parent.name: King's Gambit
parent.overview: 2.f4 offers a pawn at once to deflect Black's e-pawn, build a big centre with d4, develop quickly and use the half-open f-file against f7 (Bc4, Nf3, castling). The root covers both the Accepted lines (2...exf4: Kieseritzky 3.Nf3 g5 4.h4 g4 5.Ne5, Muzio, Bishop's Gambit 3.Bc4) and Declined lines (Falkbeer 2...d5, Classical 2...Bc5, and 2...d6 which is the most played move in the database). Accepted lines are sharp and tactically dense; Black tries to hold the pawn with ...g5 or return it with ...d5/...d6 to ease development. Declined lines are more solid and are chosen by stronger players who want to avoid the chaos. Play is open and double-edged for White's king as well.

parent.name: Englund Gambit
parent.overview: Black answers 1.d4 with 1...e5, offering the e-pawn after 2.dxe5 to avoid closed queen's-pawn positions and set tactical problems. The main line is 2...Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7 4.Bf4 Qb4+ 5.Bd2 Qxb2 6.Nc3, where Black regains the pawn on b2 but loses the queenside attack; the gambit relies on traps such as 6.Bc3?? Bb4! with mate threats on c1. White can simply keep the pawn and, with accurate development, retains an advantage. Strong players and engines consider it unsound for Black, and top-level players almost never choose it. It scores through quick development and traps against an unprepared opponent.

parent.name: King's Indian Attack
parent.overview: White builds the mirror image of the King's Indian Defence: Nf3, g3, Bg2, O-O, d3, Nbd2 and e4, usually against any Black set-up, particularly ...d5 with ...e6 or ...c5. The central pawn push e4-e5 gives a kingside bind and space, after which White expands with h4-h5, g4 and knight manoeuvres (Nf1-e3/g3 or Ne1-g2) towards a kingside attack. Black generally seeks counterplay on the queenside with ...c5, ...b5 or ...a5, or contests e4 directly. It has a modest theory load and keeps the same ideas whatever Black plays, so it is popular at club level, though it is uncommon among top grandmasters today. Black's main dilemma is that passive play lets White have a superior version of the King's Indian Defence, while ...e5 can leave Black behind in development.

parent.name: Scandinavian Defense: Main Line
parent.moves: 1. e4 d5 2. exd5 Qxd5 3. Nc3 Qa5 4. d4 Nf6
parent.overview: After 3...Qa5 Black keeps the queen out of reach of Nc3 tempo gains, pins down Nc3 on the a5-e1 diagonal, and aims for a Caro-Kann-like shell: ...Nf6, ...c6, ...Bf5 or ...Bg4, ...e6, ...Bd6 or ...Be7, often castling long onto the half-open d-file. White gets a lead in space and development (the cost to Black is a tempo, as the queen has moved twice), plays d4, Nf3, Bc4 and Bd2, and can castle either side. The standard main line runs 4.d4 c6 5.Nf3 Nf6 6.Bc4 Bf5 7.Bd2 e6 with 8.Qe2 or 8.O-O. Play is steady and positional, with fewer forced lines than the Sicilian or 1...e5 openings. It is a repertoire pick for Black players wanting clear structures.

parent.name: Scotch Game
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4
parent.overview: White strikes at the centre on move three and, after 3...exd4 4.Nxd4, trades the d-pawn for Black's e-pawn, opening the position early and releasing the central tension (s2). White gets space and quick development, Black gets easy piece play and the choice between active set-ups: 4...Bc5 (Classical), 4...Nf6 (Schmidt) and, less often, 4...Qh4 (Steinitz). The structure is open from the outset, so the game turns on piece activity rather than pawn manoeuvring. It can be played either positionally or tactically depending on the line (s2, s3). Objectively roughly equal: the Classical and Schmidt lines give Black good chances of equality, while Mieses (5.Nxc6 bxc6 6.e5) and the Steinitz are sharper (s1). Kasparov revived it in the 1990s as a way of avoiding the heavy Ruy Lopez theory, and Carlsen, Kramnik and Aronian have used it since (s1, s2, s3).

parent.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit
parent.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. e4 dxe4 3. Nc3 Nf6
parent.overview: White offers a pawn with 1.d4 d5 2.e4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3, aiming for rapid development, the open f-file and a kingside attack with Bc4, Nge2 or Bf4, castling, g4/h4 and Qe1-h4 ideas against h7. Black accepts with 4...exf3 5.Nxf3 and can choose among the Euwe (5...e6), Ziegler (5...c6), Teichmann (5...Bg4) and Bogoljubov (5...g6) defences, or decline with the Lemberger Countergambit 3...e5. With accurate defence Black consolidates the pawn, trades pieces and heads for a better endgame; engines and master opinion call White's compensation insufficient, which is why it is almost never seen at top level. Below master level it scores very well because the attack is easy to play and hard to defend against. The game is typically open and tactical.

parent.name: Scandinavian Defense: Modern Variation
parent.overview: Black answers 2.exd5 by developing the knight and delaying the recapture, avoiding the tempo lost when the queen takes on d5. The main line is 3.d4 Nxd5 (the Marshall, as the old name had it), after which 4.Nf3 and 4.c4 Nb6 or ...Bg4 give White a space edge and Black quick development and easy piece play. White can also hold the pawn with 3.c4 (Black strikes back with ...c6 into Panov-type structures, or the Icelandic Gambit 3...e6) or play 3.Bb5+ Bd7. Wikipedia/Emms describe the 2...Nf6 lines as the more tactical branch of the Scandinavian, though sound for Black; White usually keeps a slight initiative through development. Positions are usually open or semi-open with Caro-Kann-like pawn formations (...c6, ...e6) and Black often castles short while White controls more space.

parent.name: Ruy Lopez
parent.overview: The Ruy Lopez is the most extensively developed Open Game. 3.Bb5 attacks the knight that defends e5, building indirect pressure on the e5 pawn without the Italian's vulnerability to ...d5. This root (3.Bb5) is a crossroads: after the most common 3...a6 (about two-thirds of games) the Closed Spanish (4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3) leads to a slow, locked-centre manoeuvring game; the Berlin (3...Nf6 4.O-O Nxe4) gives a solid, drawish endgame-flavoured structure; the Marshall Attack is a sharp Black pawn sacrifice. White's central plan is c3 and d4 plus the Nbd2-f1-g3 knight route, while Black counterattacks on the queenside (...b5, ...Na5, ...c5) or breaks with ...d5. Theory is the deepest of any 1.e4 opening.
